Installation

How to install a SATOM node — requirements and sizing, the connected and air-gapped (offline bundle) installs per distribution family, Docker, standalone or two-node cluster, what the installer sets up, and how to finish the install by arming the protections.

👤 ForAdministratorAdvanced user
📍 WhereServer shell — installers/install-satom.sh, installers/satom-setup.sh, offline bundles, deploy/docker/

Overview#

One interactive installer, two modes — connected (online) and air-gapped (offline bundle). It asks for the IP, the port, the admin password and standalone or cluster, and handles everything else: packages, PostgreSQL, the internal PKI, the systemd services and nginx TLS.

Every installation path ends in the same state: the console on https://, plain http:// answering with a 301 redirect, the application running as an unprivileged service account, and the background services enabled.

💡Tip — Step-by-step on GitHub

The installation manual (docs/INSTALL.md, also shipped inside every offline bundle) walks through it in order: §1 requirements, §2 the ways to install (online, the offline bundle for Debian 12, RHEL 9 and openSUSE Leap 15, or Docker), §3 every question the installer asks, §4 joining a second node, §5 the permissions to request from your systems team and §6 what to do after installing. The installer scripts are in installers/ and the offline bundles are attached to each release — the newest is the latest release.

Path Use when Entry point
Guided You want one script to check the machine and drive either path below satom-setup.sh
Native, online The node can reach the distribution mirrors, PyPI and the code repository install-satom.sh
Native, offline The management network has no Internet access offline bundle → install-satom.sh
Docker The host runs containers rather than services deploy/docker/

Requirements#

Operating system#

  • A Linux distribution with systemd as PID 1. Alpine/musl is not supported.
  • Supported families (package manager detected automatically): Debian / Ubuntu (apt), RHEL / Rocky / Alma / Fedora (dnf/yum), openSUSE / SLES (zypper), Arch (pacman). Debian 12 is the reference platform.
  • Python 3.10 or later; the installer installs the distribution's own if it is missing.
  • Root, or an account allowed by sudo to run the installer (see Security model).

The installer installs, from the distribution's repositories only: Python, PostgreSQL, nginx, rsync, OpenSSL, CA certificates, curl, sudo and git (online only), plus the SSH client and server in cluster mode only. Python libraries go into /opt/satom/venv, never into the system Python.

Ports#

Port Use Reached by
Console port (default 443) HTTPS console operators
80/tcp Redirect to HTTPS and ACME HTTP challenge operators, the ACME CA if used
8443/tcp Node-to-node health probes the other node (cluster)
5432/tcp PostgreSQL replication the other node (cluster)
22/tcp data/ sync over SSH the other node (cluster)
outbound HTTPS / SSH to the appliances this node → appliances

Sizing#

Tier Devices Server policies per device vCPU RAM Disk
Lab / PoC ≤ 10 ≤ 100 2 4 GB 20 GB
Small ≤ 25 ≤ 250 4 4 GB 30 GB
Medium ≤ 60 ≤ 250 4 8 GB 40 GB
Large ≤ 110 ≤ 750 8 8 GB 120 GB

The absolute minimum to complete an installation is 2 vCPU, 2 GB RAM and 15 GB disk. Beyond about 110 devices one node cannot finish its 3-minute collection window — split the fleet across installations. The disk column assumes the default retention (396 days of metrics).

⚠️Warning — Keep free space

Always keep at least max(15 % of the volume, 3 GB) free and alert on it. A full disk puts PostgreSQL into a crash loop while /healthz still answers 200.

Advanced How the sizing limits are derived
  • Device count is bound by device I/O, not by CPU, RAM or disk. Collection costs about 0.82 s of appliance I/O per device in each 3-minute window (measured on a LAN). The ceiling is D_max = (window × duty) / 0.82 s: at a 50 % duty cycle that is about 110 devices, which is where the Large tier stops. Keep the margin — one unreachable appliance spends its full connect timeout inside the window.
  • Server policies add little I/O because the policy status of a device is read in one call for all its policies; they mainly cost disk.
  • Disk grows with server policies far more than with devices. Measured constants: about 1.66 KB per stored configuration-object row (roughly 0.45 MB of configuration index per server policy) against 1.08 bytes per stored metric sample, so at scale the configuration index outgrows the metric history about 2:1. The source-of-truth store grows with configuration changes, not with device count, because an unchanged configuration writes nothing.
  • The full derivation, with every constant's provenance and how to re-measure it on your own node, ships with the product as docs/sizing.md.

Check first#

sudo bash install-satom.sh --preflight     # or --check; changes nothing
sudo bash satom-setup.sh --check

The preflight verifies writable system paths, free space, busy ports (and which process holds them), required tools, the bundle (offline) and whether SATOM is already running. It refuses to install over an active node unless SATOM_ALLOW_REINSTALL=1 is set, because a reinstall writes a new .env; use Software update to upgrade instead.

Native installation#

The same install-satom.sh serves both modes: it installs online when it runs on its own, and offline when it finds a bundle/ directory beside it.

OnlineAny distro family

🌐Connected install

Fetches OS packages from the distribution mirrors and Python wheels from PyPI as it goes, and clones the project's public repository (the URL can be changed at the prompt). It detects apt, dnf/yum, zypper or pacman and maps package names per family; PostgreSQL's data directory, configuration file and pg_hba.conf are queried from the running engine itself, so the Debian, RHEL, SUSE and Arch layouts all work.

# step 0 — reports, changes nothing
sudo bash install-satom.sh --preflight
# then, as root on a fresh host
sudo bash install-satom.sh
  • Checks the required packages first: what is missing is installed, and an outdated version is reported before it is upgraded.
  • Requires systemd and Python 3.10 or later. Where the distribution's default Python is older (RHEL 9 ships 3.9), a newer one from the distribution's own repositories is installed automatically (python3.11 on RHEL 9).

OfflineDebian 12RHEL 9openSUSE 15

📦Air-gapped install

Self-contained bundles, one per distribution family — OS packages, Python wheels and the application — for hosts with no Internet access. The installer auto-detects bundle/, never touches the network, and refuses a bundle built for the wrong family with a clear message before anything is changed.

# Debian 12
tar xzf satom-offline-<version>-debian12-amd64.tar.gz
# RHEL / Rocky / AlmaLinux 9
tar xzf satom-offline-<version>-rhel9-x86_64.tar.gz
# openSUSE Leap 15 / SLES 15
tar xzf satom-offline-<version>-suse15-x86_64.tar.gz

cd satom-installer
sudo bash install-satom.sh
  • Debian 12 bundle: the full .deb dependency closure, plus the Python wheels.
  • RHEL / Rocky / Alma 9 bundle: a local dnf repository (with metadata) plus the wheels for Python 3.11 (python3.11 included) — dnf resolves only what the host actually needs.
  • openSUSE Leap / SLES 15 bundle: a local zypper repository in a directory of its own; zypper uses it without touching or registering the system repositories. The two RPM bundles exist side by side and are deliberately not interchangeable — different package names and base libraries — so the wrong one is refused up front instead of failing halfway through.
  • Every bundle carries the ACME client and the sudo and SSH packages — a host with no network cannot fetch them mid-install.
  • A bundle is a snapshot of the product at build time and records its own version: the safeguards it installs are the ones of the version it contains.

Offline bundle details#

  • Arch has no offline bundle; install it online.
  • Besides the packages, a bundle carries the application, the ACME client, the metrics-store binary, the release's API library pack, the sudo and SSH packages and the sysadmin manual INSTALL.md. Verify it with the .sha256 file shipped beside it.
  • To read the version a bundle contains before installing it:

bash tar xzOf satom-offline-<version>-*.tar.gz --wildcards '*/bundle/app.tar.gz' | tar xzO VERSION - Bundles are built with installers/build-offline-bundle.sh (on Debian 12), build-offline-bundle-rhel.sh (on Rocky 9) and build-offline-bundle-suse.sh (on openSUSE Leap 15.6), each with network access. - The browser does not need the Internet either: every script, stylesheet and font is served by the node.

What the installer asks#

  1. The node's IP address (auto-detected).
  2. The HTTPS port of the console (default 443).
  3. The DNS name(s) the console is reached by (default: hostname -f; commas or spaces separate several). They become the nginx server_name and the subject alternative names of the node certificate, and the machine's short host name is added automatically. A name left out here produces a browser name-mismatch warning and means reissuing the certificate later, so give every name operators will type. SATOM_SERVED_NAMES answers this question in an unattended install.
  4. Standalone or cluster; for a cluster, primary or secondary. A primary asks for the planned IP of the secondary (Enter allows the whole subnet); a secondary asks for the join key, which is validated before anything is installed.
  5. The password of the console's admin user (standalone and primary only; 12 to 1024 characters, length only — the same rule as every other password path in SATOM).
  6. A summary to confirm. Nothing is changed before this point.

It then installs, in order: packages → code and virtual environment → PostgreSQL → PKI and certificates → services and nginx → health check.

  1. 1Preflightnothing changed yet
  2. 2QuestionsIP, port, topology, admin password
  3. 3Packagesfrom the mirrors or the bundle
  4. 4Application/opt/satom, venv, .env (root:satom 0640)
  5. 5DatabasePostgreSQL, database satom; replica on a secondary
  6. 6TLSinternal CA, node certificate, nginx vhost
  7. 7Servicesunits, drop-ins, timers, CLI, root-owned update runner
  8. 8Health checksummary; the join key on a primary

What the installer sets up#

Component Detail
Packages Python ≥ 3.10, PostgreSQL, nginx, rsync, OpenSSL and the rest of the list under Requirements — installed or upgraded per distribution family
Application Code in /opt/satom with its own virtual environment; pinned dependencies from the bundle's wheels (offline) or PyPI (online)
Database PostgreSQL cluster initialised if needed; the application database, roles and schema created; streaming replication on a cluster
PKI Internal CA on the primary (or standalone node); a certificate per node; nginx TLS on the chosen port
Services systemd units for the web application and the scheduler, the reconciler and the metrics store; the alert, certificate-renewal and responder timers; the integration and update triggers; the data/ sync timer on a cluster — enabled, then checked through /healthz
Accounts A dedicated, shell-less service account owns the tree and runs the units; a single root-owned runner handles updates. The web application does not run as root
Operator CLI The satom console, installed as a root-owned copy outside the application tree (/usr/local/sbin/satom) and re-installed by every update
Host integration SELinux booleans and port labels applied best-effort when enforcing; the console port and 80/tcp (plus 5432/tcp on a cluster primary) opened in firewalld or ufw when either is active
  • A sysadmin manual (INSTALL.md) ships inside every bundle: requirements, the exact package lists per distribution family, the permissions to request, the three separate sudo policies (installer, service account, operator) and the sudoers options, a hardening checklist and the uninstall procedure.
  • Re-running the installer is not an upgrade path: on a node where SATOM is already active the preflight refuses, because a reinstall rewrites .env and the units (see Check first). Upgrade through Software update.

Unattended installs#

  • SATOM_SERVED_NAMES — host names the node answers to (certificate SAN and nginx server_name; default hostname -f).
  • SATOM_APP_USER — service-account name (default satom).
  • SATOM_API_PACK=none skips importing the API library pack; SATOM_API_PACK_PRODUCTS=fortiweb,fortiadc limits it.
  • satom-setup.sh --yes --answers answers.env answers every question from SETUP_* variables (satom-setup.sh --help lists them).

Standalone or two-node cluster#

A standalone node needs nothing more than the steps above. Cluster setup is part of the same installer run — there is no separate procedure.

1️⃣Install the primary

Choose cluster → primary. At the end the installer prints a one-line join key, starting with SATOMJOIN1., that encodes everything the secondary needs.

2️⃣Join the secondary

Run the same installer on the second host, choose cluster → secondary, and paste the key. Streaming replication, the shared secrets and the data sync configure themselves: the secondary inherits the encryption keys, clones the database and becomes a streaming replica, and generates its own SSH key for the data sync.

3️⃣Certificates mint locally

The secondary receives the cluster's internal CA through the join key and issues its own node certificate locally during installation — the node's private key never travels between nodes.

One step remains: on the primary, authorise the secondary's public key with the command the secondary prints:

sudo bash install-satom.sh --authorize-peer <standby-ip> "ssh-ed25519 AAAA..."

Until then the database replicates but the data/ sync fails.

⚠️Warning — The join key is a secret

It contains the internal CA private key, FERNET_KEY, SECRET_KEY and the database passwords. Move it over a secure channel, use it once, delete it.

The secondary's scheduler stays idle until it is promoted. See High availability.

Docker#

cd deploy/docker
cp env.example .env
./satom-docker.sh gen-secrets
./satom-docker.sh build satom:<version>
./satom-docker.sh up

The stack runs the application, PostgreSQL, Redis, the metrics store and an nginx proxy; web, scheduler and cron are the same image. satom-setup.sh can also perform a Docker install (secrets in /opt/satom-docker/satom.env, mode 0600 — back it up).

A container does not administer its host, so Software Update, service control, certificate activation and systemd unit health are refused in the console with a message naming the alternative — unless the optional operations agent (compose.agent.yaml) is enabled, which brings them back under Container operations. HA promotion is refused in either case.

Two container nodes#

A production pair is a primary and a standby, not two halves of a load balancer: the standby's PostgreSQL is a streaming replica, its scheduler and cron services idle until the database is promoted (so two nodes never fire the same action), and your reverse proxy should carry it as a backup server that takes traffic only when the primary stops answering /healthz.

  1. On the primary, set SATOM_NODE_ROLE=primary and an immutable SATOM_IMAGE tag in .env, then run SATOM_ENV=prod ./satom-docker.sh up.
  2. Copy the same .env to the standby — SECRET_KEY, FERNET_KEY and the database passwords must match, or the standby replicates credentials it cannot decrypt — and change SATOM_NODE_ROLE=standby and SATOM_PRIMARY_HOST=<primary address>.
  3. Run SATOM_ENV=prod ./satom-docker.sh up on the standby. It takes a base backup of the primary on first start and then follows it.

satom-docker.sh refuses the standby role without SATOM_PRIMARY_HOST. After a failover the promoted node refuses to start under the standby role again: it holds every write accepted since the failover, so rebuilding it from the old primary is left to an explicit operator decision.

A node without registry access#

Move the image as a file, the same way the offline bundles travel:

./satom-docker.sh export satom:<version> /tmp/satom-<version>.tar.gz   # writes a .sha256 beside it
# copy the tarball AND its .sha256 to the target, then
./satom-docker.sh import /tmp/satom-<version>.tar.gz

import checks the .sha256 before loading the image, so a truncated copy is reported as a checksum failure rather than as a layer error inside docker load. Without the .sha256 beside the tarball it only warns that it cannot verify.

What a container backup must cover#

The image is disposable; the satom-data volume is not. It holds the device backup vault, the system backup bundles, the configuration-history object store and the reports. Back it up together with a database dump: the history index lives in PostgreSQL while its objects live in the volume, so a database dump restored alone leaves rows pointing at nothing.

The reverse proxy#

The installer writes the nginx vhost for you (TLS 1.2/1.3, HSTS, client_max_body_size 400M, proxy_read_timeout 120s). If you put SATOM behind your own proxy or load balancer, it must pass:

proxy_set_header Host              $http_host;   # NOT $host
proxy_set_header X-Forwarded-For   $proxy_add_x_forwarded_for;
proxy_set_header X-Forwarded-Proto $scheme;

$host drops the port: behind a non-standard port every form, including the sign-in form, then fails with a "session expired" message. Also add the proxy's address to TRUSTED_PROXIES so rate limits and the audit log see the real client address. See Security model.

First sign-in#

Installed with admin password
install-satom.sh the one you typed at the prompt
satom-setup.sh typed (12 to 1024 characters, no character-class rule) or, if left empty, generated into /root/satom-admin-password.txt (0600)
Application start-up on an empty database SATOM_ADMIN_PASSWORD, or a random password written to /opt/satom/initial-admin-password (0600)

There is no default password. See First login.

ℹ️Note

Changed in 2.11.0: both installers apply the console's single password rule (at least 12 characters, at most 1024, no character classes); before, install-satom.sh accepted 8 characters and satom-setup.sh asked for 10 with three character classes. The legacy deploy/install.sh script has been removed.

After installing#

curl -k https://satom.example.com/healthz              # 200
systemctl status satom satom-scheduler
satom diagnose install       # is this node armed, or merely installed?
satom diagnose all

Finishing the install: arm the protections#

The safeguards travel with the code; the coverage does not — and this is the most common way an installation ends up unprotected.

Required

🗓️Nothing is scheduled until the first appliance

Schedules are database rows, the seeds are insert-only and an operator's edit always wins over them. A brand-new node has no scheduled actions and no alert recipient. When it gets its first appliance, SATOM creates the default System Automations (the plan below) — only while the node has none at all; rows you deleted are not re-created. The alert recipient is never created for you: without it, signals are computed and delivered nowhere.

# show the gap (any user), then close it
satom diagnose install
sudo satom execute seed actions           # print the plan; changes nothing
sudo satom execute seed actions --yes     # create the missing actions
  • Prints the plan first and only fills gaps — a schedule that already exists is never touched. Run it on the primary (or standalone node); a standby refuses, and replication carries the rows to it.
  • The recommended set: hourly device sync, nightly inspection and system backup, probe sweep and metrics scrape every 3 minutes, a daily inventory snapshot, daily/weekly/monthly reports and the Sentinel jobs.
  • Set an alert recipient under Settings → Email & Alerts — a computed signal with nowhere to go is not an alert — and configure the Backup Server, so that copies do not live only inside the same nodes.

Recommended

🔑Grant the operator account, not root

Day-to-day diagnosis and repair run through the satom console, which needs one entry in the sudo policy for a person's account — a single binary at a fixed path, owned by root. The CLI prints the rule itself, with no privilege required, so it can be handed to a systems team without shipping the repository.

satom show sudoers <account>    # prints the rule; changes nothing
satom diagnose privilege        # then verify the sudo boundary is intact
  • The path must stay fixed and the binary root-owned — a writable target makes the rule equivalent to unrestricted root.
  • The check fails if the CLI was granted to the service account, which would be the same mistake.
  • Without the rule, get, show and diagnose still work for any user; only execute needs root.

Hardening checklist#

  1. Arm the protections as described above.
  2. Remove the installer permission: rm /etc/sudoers.d/satom-installer.
  3. Restrict the console port to the operations networks.
  4. Check the privilege model:

bash systemctl show satom.service -p User --value # the service account, not root sudo -u satom sudo -n nginx -t # allowed sudo -u satom sudo -n systemctl restart satom # must fail

  1. Replace the self-signed certificate when ready, in Node TLS or with deploy/tls-bootstrap.sh import-cert --cert FILE --key FILE.
  2. Secure the recovery secrets (sudo satom execute seal recovery). See Security model.

Logs: /var/log/satom/, /var/log/satom-install.log and journalctl -u satom.

Advanced No legacy deploy/install.sh

The old development bootstrap deploy/install.sh (root service, SQLite database) is no longer shipped. Install with installers/install-satom.sh or the guided installers/satom-setup.sh.
